item.title: The App lifecycle
item.description:
Every humus application is a bedrock.App, and the root package’s humus.App is the lifecycle every humus service runs. It reads its settings, listens for signals, builds its telemetry and the user’s dependencies, runs one or more Services, drains and shuts them down within a grace period, releases what was built, shuts its telemetry down and turns the outcome into an exit status.

A service’s main is func main() { humus.Main(app.Init) }, where app.Init is the end user’s Init. humus.Main builds the humus.App from its defaults and that Init, applies the options it is given, and runs the App on the OS process. Options change the App’s fields, so everything this page says about humus.App is what Main runs. The runtime packages — REST, gRPC, jobs, queues — export Services for Init to return, not Apps, and one whose Services need a drain wraps Main with defaults of its own: see Runtime packages. An App that mixes runtimes, such as a REST API and a gRPC service in one process, needs nothing more.

item.title: Serving HTTP
item.description:
The httpserver package serves an http.Handler over TLS as a humus.Service. The end user’s Init sources its Settings, builds the Service with httpserver.NewService and returns it, and httpserver.Main runs it with the defaults an HTTP server behind a load balancer needs: a 5s drain and a 10s grace period. Its test package, httpservertest, runs the same App in a test, on the same defaults, with an HTTP/2 client.

The package is the server half of what rest.Run did before the reset, without the REST DSL, which is openapi/v3 now. It exports no App, runs no health Service and serves no probes: httphealth answers them, as Health probes describes. The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: HTTP server foundation, with its revision 1 and revision 2.

item.title: Serving an API with OpenAPI
item.description:
The openapi/v3 package serves an API of typed operations, and its OpenAPI document. The end user’s Init declares each operation once, on a typed path, with a typed handler and the codecs of its bodies, builds the API with openapi.NewAPI, and hands it to httpserver.NewService, which serves it over TLS as Serving HTTP describes. The same declarations serve the requests and write the document, so the two can’t disagree.

The import path names the major version of OpenAPI the package follows, and the package’s name is openapi. Two packages beside it are opt-in, and openapi uses neither: jsoncodec reads and writes JSON bodies, and problem answers errors with RFC 9457 problem details. The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: OpenAPI endpoint DSL, as its revisions 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 amend it.

item.title: Calling HTTP services
item.description:
The httpclient package calls another service over HTTP. httpclient.NewClient builds a client for one dependency in the end user’s Init, from Settings the end user sources, and returns a plain *http.Client. Its calls go through the Setup’s Host, are traced and measured with the Setup’s telemetry, are retried when that is safe, and fail at once while a circuit breaker says the dependency keeps failing.

Service code, generated clients and SDKs take the *http.Client as they take any other, and depend on net/http’s type rather than on this package, so a unit test of that code passes any client. The client dials only through the Setup’s Host, so a test runs the end user’s whole App, its outbound calls included, on humustest’s network, as Testing shows.

item.title: Health
item.description:
A service reports its health as monitors it combines into two probes, liveness and readiness, and an App’s readiness is owned by a health Service it returns from Init like any other Service. All of it is in the health package, which depends on nothing but the standard library and serves no protocol. httphealth and grpc/grpchealth expose the probes to Kubernetes.

The design behind this page is in Proposal: health monitors and probes, Revision 2, and, for exposing the probes, in Proposal: exposing health probes.

item.title: Jobs
item.description:
A job is a process that does one piece of work and exits. The job package turns that work, the run, into a humus.Service that runs it once, stops it on either shutdown signal and records one span around it. The job runs on humus.Main’s defaults, and the run’s error is the exit status, so Kubernetes retries a job that failed or was interrupted and completes one that finished.

The package is job.NewService and nothing else: no App, no Main, no Settings. The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: jobs and its revision.

item.title: Consuming and producing Kafka
item.description:
The queue/kafka package consumes Kafka topics as a humus.Service, with franz-go. The Service joins a consumer group, dials the brokers through the Setup’s Host, and hands each record to the end user’s queue.Processor, one record at a time per partition, in offset order. The end user’s Init sources its Settings, builds the Service with kafka.NewService, and returns it to humus.Main, whose defaults are a consumer’s.

The package produces records too. A kafka.Producer, which the end user’s Init builds with kafka.NewProducer, produces to one cluster for any Service of the process: a Processor that produces a dead letter or writes to another topic, an HTTP handler that publishes an event, a job. Producing describes it.

item.title: Consuming and publishing with RabbitMQ
item.description:
The queue/rabbitmq package consumes a RabbitMQ queue as a humus.Service, with amqp091-go, RabbitMQ’s own Go client. The Service dials the broker through the Setup’s Host, consumes one queue with manual acks, and hands each delivery to the end user’s queue.Processor, in the order the queue delivered them. The end user’s Init sources its Settings, builds the Service with rabbitmq.NewService, and returns it to humus.Main, whose defaults are a consumer’s.

The package publishes too. A rabbitmq.Publisher, which the end user’s Init builds with rabbitmq.NewPublisher, publishes to the broker with publisher confirms for any Service of the process: a Processor that publishes an event, an HTTP handler, a job. Publishing describes it.

item.title: gRPC services
item.description: The grpcserver package serves gRPC over TLS as a humus.Service. The end user’s Init sources its Settings, builds the Service with grpcserver.NewService, registers their generated services on it, as they would on a *grpc.Server, and returns it. grpcserver.Main runs it with the defaults a gRPC server behind a Kubernetes Service needs: a 5s drain and a 15s grace period. Its test package, grpcservertest, runs the same App in a test, on the same defaults, with a client that dials the test Host over TLS.

item.title: Calling gRPC services
item.description: The grpcclient package calls another service over gRPC. grpcclient.NewClient builds a Client for one dependency in the end user’s Init, from Settings the end user sources. The Client is a grpc.ClientConnInterface, so generated code takes it as it takes a *grpc.ClientConn. Its calls go through the Setup’s Host, are traced and measured with the Setup’s telemetry, are retried as the end user’s Classify decides, and fail at once while a circuit breaker says the dependency keeps failing.

item.title: Authentication and authorization
item.description: The auth package authenticates and authorizes the requests a humus service serves, over HTTP and gRPC alike. A scheme is a typed value whose verify function turns a request’s credential into the end user’s own principal, which a handler reads back with the scheme’s From. A requirement is what a request must have: a scheme, a scheme with scopes, several schemes, or nothing at all. Three places enforce requirements, one for each way humus serves requests: openapi.Security for an OpenAPI API, auth.NewHandler for a plain http.Handler served by httpserver, and grpcauth’s Interceptors for a grpcserver Service.

item.title: Configuring a humus service
item.description: humus packages are configured with plain Go values. They read no environment variables for their settings, define no variable names and read no files on your behalf; the few variables humus does read are listed below. Every value is sourced in your own Init, with whatever names and formats your service already uses: an environment variable called READ_TIMEOUT or MYSVC_HTTP_READ_TIMEOUT, a duration written 5s, a file of PEM, a flag. The usual tool is bedrock’s config package, and this page uses it throughout.

item.title: Telemetry
item.description:
A humus App builds its OpenTelemetry providers before Init, hands them to Init as one value, logs through them, and shuts them down last. The telemetry package builds them from a plain Settings value. humus.Main builds them from telemetry.DefaultSettings() unless the service passes a Builder of its own, which sources that value the same way Init sources any other package’s settings.

The design behind everything on this page is in Proposal: OpenTelemetry without globals, Revision 2. The lifecycle describes when the App builds its telemetry and shuts it down.

item.title: Testing a humus App
item.description:
A humus App runs whole inside a test. humustest makes that possible:

  • humustest.Start hands the end user’s Init to the App that humus.Main would run for it, with the same defaults, on a test Host in place of humus.OSHost() and on a new process from bedrocktest: its arguments, environment and stdin, which the test sets, its output, which the test reads, and its signals, which the test sends. It returns the process and a channel for the App’s exit status.
  • a Host, whose in-memory network the App listens on and the test dials, and whose filesystem is confined to the test’s own temp directory;
  • a certificate authority, NewCA, generated for each test;
  • Telemetry, a recorder of what an App emits, covered on the Telemetry page;
  • and TestService, the contract every Service must pass.

The network opens no real socket and starts no goroutines, so the App runs in a testing/synctest bubble. It needs no real environment, no real time and no file outside the test’s temp directory.

item.title: Failure injection
item.description: Failure injection lets one request fail on purpose, in production or in a test, without failing anyone else’s. A request carries a failure scenario in its OpenTelemetry baggage, and every injection point the request passes through, such as a call to a dependency, looks itself up in the scenario and learns whether to fail or slow down. The end user then sees how the whole service copes with a dependency that is down or slow: its retries, its breakers and its fallbacks.

item.title: Writing a Kubernetes controller
item.description: The kube package writes Kubernetes controllers as humus.Services, with client-go, Kubernetes’ own client, and no controller-runtime. It reaches the API server through the Setup’s Host, declares custom resources as Go values, reflects their CRDs from Go types, and reconciles their objects, or those of Kubernetes’ own kinds, on client-go’s informers, work queue and leader election. The end user’s Init fills a kube.Connection and sources kube.Settings, builds a Client and a Reconciler, and returns the Service that kube.NewController builds to humus.Main, whose defaults fit a controller.

item.title: Calling the provider
item.description:
The provider is invented for the walkthrough, and is one endpoint: POST /v1/messages, with a bearer key, an Idempotency-Key, and the sender, recipient, subject and text as JSON. It answers 2xx with the email’s id, or a 4xx with a reason.

item.title: The projection
item.description:
The projection keeps every event it applied, and each order’s status, folded from its events. The store package reads and writes it, and the projector package folds it.

The schema

store/schema.sql:

CREATE TABLE order_events (
 source_partition integer NOT NULL,
 source_offset bigint NOT NULL,
 order_id text NOT NULL,
 type text NOT NULL,
 at timestamptz NOT NULL,
 PRIMARY KEY (source_partition, source_offset)
);

CREATE INDEX order_events_by_order ON order_events (order_id, at);

CREATE TABLE order_status (
 order_id text PRIMARY KEY,
 status text NOT NULL,
 at timestamptz NOT NULL
);

An event is keyed by the partition and offset it was consumed from on orders.events, so a redelivery is found by them.

item.title: Init
item.description:
The settings

Everything Init reads, in one struct:

type settings struct {
	Database *pgxpool.Config
	Payments httpclient.Settings
	APIKey string
	Period time.Time
	Concurrency int
}

config.Struct sources and checks each one. A bad one makes Init fail, and the job exits 78, naming its variable:

func readSettings(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) (settings, error) {
	env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) }
	file := func(name string) config.Value[[]byte] { return env(name).Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)) }

	return config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) settings {
		client := httpclient.DefaultSettings()
		client.BaseURL = r.Get(env("PAYMENTS_URL").Parse(url.Parse).Validate(checkPaymentsURL))
		client.TLS = r.Get(file("PAYMENTS_CA_FILE").Parse(certPool).Default(nil).Map(func(roots *x509.CertPool) *tls.Config {
			return &tls.Config{RootCAs: roots}
		}).Validate(httpclient.CheckTLS))
		client.Timeout = r.Get(env("PAYMENTS_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(client.Timeout).Validate(httpclient.CheckTimeout))
		client.AttemptTimeout = r.Get(env("PAYMENTS_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(client.AttemptTimeout).Validate(httpclient.CheckAttemptTimeout))
		client.MaxAttempts = r.Get(env("PAYMENTS_MAX_ATTEMPTS").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(client.MaxAttempts).Validate(httpclient.CheckMaxAttempts))

		return settings{
			Database: r.Get(file("DATABASE_URL_FILE").Parse(databaseURL)),
			Payments: client,
			APIKey: r.Get(file("PAYMENTS_API_KEY_FILE").Parse(apiKey)),
			Period: r.Get(env("BILLING_PERIOD").Parse(parseMonth).Default(lastMonth(time.Now())).Validate(checkEnded)),
			Concurrency: r.Get(env("BILLING_CONCURRENCY").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(4).Validate(checkConcurrency)),
		}
	}).Read(ctx)
}
Variable What it is Default
DATABASE_URL_FILE a file holding the PostgreSQL URL, password included required
PAYMENTS_URL the payments API’s base URL, https required
PAYMENTS_API_KEY_FILE a file holding the API key required
PAYMENTS_CA_FILE the CA certificates the API is trusted through, PEM the system’s roots
PAYMENTS_TIMEOUT, PAYMENTS_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT, PAYMENTS_MAX_ATTEMPTS httpclient.Settings’ fields httpclient.DefaultSettings()'
BILLING_PERIOD the month to issue, YYYY-MM, which has ended last month, in UTC
BILLING_CONCURRENCY charges in flight, 1 to 32 4

The secrets, as files

The database URL and the API key are files mounted from Secrets, read through the Host’s FS, so the tests can give the job files of their own:

item.title: Retries and dead letters
item.description:
Parking a request

A request that failed for now is published to mail.retry, with its attempt one higher. A returned error would stop the Service instead, and every replica would crash-loop through a provider’s outage:

func (w *Worker) park(ctx context.Context, m rabbitmq.Message, attempt int) error {
	p := request(m, mail.RetryExchange, map[string]any{
		mail.AttemptHeader: int64(attempt),
	})
	p.UserID = w.user
	if err := w.retries.Publish(ctx, p); err != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("worker: parking the request in %s: %w", mail.RetryExchange, err)
	}
	return nil
}

The parked request is the request as it was published, plus its headers:

item.title: Retries and dead letters
item.description:
Processing a record

One Process handles both orders.events and orders.retry, and keeps no state of its own:

func (p *Projector) Process(ctx context.Context, m kafka.Message) error {
	attempt, from, err := p.origin(m)
	if err != nil {
		return p.deadLetter(ctx, m, from, reasonMalformed, err, 0)
	}

	e, reason, err := decode(m, from)
	if err != nil {
		return p.deadLetter(ctx, m, from, reason, err, 0)
	}

	err = p.wait(ctx, m, attempt)
	if err != nil {
		return err
	}

	work, cancel := context.WithTimeout(ctx, workDeadline)
	defer cancel()
	reason, err = p.project(work, m, e)
	if err == nil {
		return nil
	}
	if ctx.Err() != nil {
		return fmt.Errorf("projecting %s, partition %d, offset %d: %w", from.topic, from.partition, from.offset, context.Cause(ctx))
	}
	return p.retry(ctx, m, from, attempt, reason, err)
}
The record Then
malformed, or of an unknown type a dead letter, at once
projected, or applied already committed
unavailable or invalid-transition, below RETRY_ATTEMPTS produced to orders.retry, one attempt higher
the same, at RETRY_ATTEMPTS a dead letter, with its last attempt’s reason
its context ended, at shutdown or a revoke Process returns the error, and the record is processed again
neither orders.retry nor orders.dlq stores it Process returns the error, and the App exits 1 
const (
	reasonMalformed = "malformed"
	reasonUnknownType = "unknown-type"
	reasonInvalidTransition = "invalid-transition"
	reasonUnavailable = "unavailable"
)

The retry headers

A retried record carries its attempt, why it failed, and where it came from on orders.events:

item.title: Init
item.description:
The settings

Everything Init reads, in one struct:

type settings struct {
	Consumer rabbitmq.Settings
	Publisher rabbitmq.PublisherSettings
	Login string
	TrustedPublishers []string
	MaxAttempts int
	Provider provider.Settings
	Probes httphealth.Settings
}

config.Struct sources and checks each one. A bad one makes Init fail, and the mailer exits 78, naming its variable:

func readSettings(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) (settings, error) {
	env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) }
	file := readFile(s.Host.FS)

	read, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) settings {
		consumer := rabbitmq.DefaultSettings()
		conn := consumer.Connection
		conn.Addr = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_ADDR").Validate(rabbitmq.CheckAddr))
		conn.Vhost = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_VHOST").Default(conn.Vhost).Validate(rabbitmq.CheckVhost))
		conn.TLS = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_CA_FILE").Parse(file).Parse(certPool).Map(trusting).Default(nil))
		login := r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_USERNAME").Validate(notEmpty))
		conn.SASL = &amqp.PlainAuth{
			Username: login,
			Password: r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_PASSWORD_FILE").Parse(file).Parse(secret)),
		}
		consumer.Connection = conn
		consumer.Queue = mail.SendQueue
		consumer.Delivery = queue.AtLeastOnce
		consumer.Prefetch = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_PREFETCH").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(defaultPrefetch).Validate(rabbitmq.CheckPrefetch))
		consumer.Concurrency = r.Get(env("RABBITMQ_CONCURRENCY").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(defaultConcurrency).Validate(rabbitmq.CheckConcurrency))

		publisher := rabbitmq.DefaultPublisherSettings()
		publisher.Connection = conn

		client := httpclient.DefaultSettings()
		return settings{
			Consumer: consumer,
			Publisher: publisher,
			Login: login,
			TrustedPublishers: r.Get(env("MAIL_TRUSTED_PUBLISHERS").Parse(logins).Default(nil)),
			MaxAttempts: r.Get(env("MAIL_MAX_ATTEMPTS").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(defaultMaxAttempts).Validate(positive)),
			Provider: provider.Settings{
				URL: r.Get(env("PROVIDER_URL").Parse(url.Parse).Validate(httpclient.CheckBaseURL)),
				CA: r.Get(env("PROVIDER_CA_FILE").Parse(file).Parse(certPool).Default(nil)),
				Timeout: r.Get(env("PROVIDER_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(client.Timeout).Validate(httpclient.CheckTimeout)),
				AttemptTimeout: r.Get(env("PROVIDER_ATTEMPT_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(client.AttemptTimeout).Validate(httpclient.CheckAttemptTimeout)),
				MaxAttempts: r.Get(env("PROVIDER_MAX_ATTEMPTS").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(client.MaxAttempts).Validate(httpclient.CheckMaxAttempts)),
				From: r.Get(env("MAIL_FROM").Validate(notEmpty)),
				APIKey: r.Get(env("PROVIDER_API_KEY_FILE").Parse(file).Parse(secret)),
			},
			Probes: httphealth.Settings{
				Addr: r.Get(env("PROBES_ADDR").Validate(httphealth.CheckAddr)),
				TLS: r.Get(env("PROBES_TLS_PEM_FILE").Parse(pemTLS(s.Host.FS)).Validate(httphealth.CheckTLS)),
			},
		}
	}).Read(ctx)
	if err != nil {
		return settings{}, err
	}

The consumer and every Publisher share one Connection, so they log in as one user.

item.title: Init
item.description:
The settings

Everything Init reads, in one struct:

type settings struct {
	Consumer kafka.Settings
	Producer kafka.ProducerSettings
	Projector projector.Settings
	Database *pgxpool.Config
	Probes httphealth.Settings
}

config.Struct sources and checks each one, with what it needs to build the rest. A bad one makes Init fail, and the processor exits 78, naming its variable:

type postgres struct {
	URL *url.URL
	Password string
	CA *x509.CertPool
}

type sourced struct {
	settings
	KafkaCA *x509.CertPool
	KafkaTLS *tls.Config
	Postgres postgres
	TrustedTopics []string
}

func readSettings(ctx context.Context, s *humus.Setup) (settings, error) {
	env := func(name string) config.Value[string] { return config.Env(s.Process.Environment, name) }
	file := func(name string) config.Value[[]byte] { return env(name).Parse(readFile(s.Host.FS)) }
	list := func(v string) []string { return strings.Split(v, ",") }

	got, err := config.Struct(func(r *config.Resolver) sourced {
		consumer := kafka.DefaultSettings()
		consumer.Brokers = r.Get(env("KAFKA_BROKERS").Map(list).Validate(kafka.CheckBrokers))
		consumer.GroupID = r.Get(env("KAFKA_GROUP_ID").Validate(kafka.CheckGroupID))
		consumer.Delivery = queue.AtLeastOnce
		consumer.SessionTimeout = r.Get(env("KAFKA_SESSION_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(consumer.SessionTimeout).Validate(kafka.CheckSessionTimeout))

		producer := kafka.DefaultProducerSettings()
		producer.DeliveryTimeout = r.Get(env("KAFKA_DELIVERY_TIMEOUT").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(producer.DeliveryTimeout).Validate(kafka.CheckDeliveryTimeout))
		producer.Breaker.OpenFor = r.Get(env("KAFKA_BREAKER_OPEN_FOR").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(producer.Breaker.OpenFor).Validate(kafka.CheckBreakerOpenFor))

		return sourced{
			settings: settings{
				Consumer: consumer,
				Producer: producer,
				Projector: projector.Settings{
					EventsTopic: r.Get(env("KAFKA_EVENTS_TOPIC").Validate(notEmpty)),
					StatusTopic: r.Get(env("KAFKA_STATUS_TOPIC").Validate(notEmpty)),
					RetryTopic: r.Get(env("KAFKA_RETRY_TOPIC").Validate(notEmpty)),
					DeadLetterTopic: r.Get(env("KAFKA_DEAD_LETTER_TOPIC").Validate(notEmpty)),
					Attempts: r.Get(env("RETRY_ATTEMPTS").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(defaultRetryAttempts).Validate(positive[int])),
					MinDelay: r.Get(env("RETRY_MIN_DELAY").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(defaultRetryMinDelay).Validate(positive[time.Duration])),
					MaxDelay: r.Get(env("RETRY_MAX_DELAY").Parse(time.ParseDuration).Default(defaultRetryMaxDelay).Validate(positive[time.Duration])),
				},
				Probes: httphealth.Settings{
					Addr: r.Get(env("PROBES_ADDR").Validate(httphealth.CheckAddr)),
					TLS: r.Get(env("PROBES_TLS_PEM_FILE").Parse(pemTLS(s.Host.FS)).Validate(httphealth.CheckTLS)),
				},
			},
			KafkaCA: r.Get(file("KAFKA_TLS_CA_FILE").Parse(certPool)),
			KafkaTLS: r.Get(env("KAFKA_TLS_CERT_FILE").Parse(pemTLS(s.Host.FS))),
			Postgres: postgres{
				URL: r.Get(env("POSTGRES_URL").Parse(parsePostgresURL).Validate(checkPostgresURL)),
				Password: r.Get(file("POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE").Parse(secret)),
				CA: r.Get(file("POSTGRES_TLS_CA_FILE").Parse(certPool)),
			},
			TrustedTopics: r.Get(env("FAULT_TRUSTED_TOPICS").Parse(topicList).Default(nil)),
		}
	}).Read(ctx)
	if err != nil {
		return settings{}, err
	}

const (
	defaultRetryAttempts = 10
	defaultRetryMinDelay = time.Second
	defaultRetryMaxDelay = 5 * time.Minute
)
Variable What it is Default
KAFKA_BROKERS the brokers’ host:ports, separated by commas required
KAFKA_GROUP_ID the consumer group required
KAFKA_EVENTS_TOPIC, KAFKA_STATUS_TOPIC, KAFKA_RETRY_TOPIC, KAFKA_DEAD_LETTER_TOPIC the four topics, each a different one required
KAFKA_TLS_CA_FILE, KAFKA_TLS_CERT_FILE the brokers’ CA, and a file holding the processor’s certificate and key, PEM required
KAFKA_SESSION_TIMEOUT kafka.Settings’ SessionTimeout kafka.DefaultSettings()'
KAFKA_DELIVERY_TIMEOUT, KAFKA_BREAKER_OPEN_FOR kafka.ProducerSettings’ DeliveryTimeout and Breaker.OpenFor kafka.DefaultProducerSettings()'
RETRY_ATTEMPTS attempts before a record is dead-lettered 10
RETRY_MIN_DELAY, RETRY_MAX_DELAY the backoff of a record’s first retry, and the longest 1s and 5m
POSTGRES_URL PostgreSQL’s URL, with its user and database, and no password required
POSTGRES_PASSWORD_FILE, POSTGRES_TLS_CA_FILE a file holding the password, and PostgreSQL’s CA required
PROBES_ADDR, PROBES_TLS_PEM_FILE the probes’ address, and a file holding their certificate and key, PEM required
FAULT_TRUSTED_TOPICS the topics whose records’ scenarios are trusted, separated by commas none
FAULT_MAX_DELAY the longest delay a scenario injects 10s

The four topics must differ, and the backoff can’t start above its longest:

item.title: Testing
item.description:
A store in memory

The unit tests give Run an Invoices of their own, which keeps the subscriptions and invoices in memory:

type store struct {
	mu sync.Mutex
	subscriptions []subscription
	invoices []*invoice
	issueErr error
	settleErr error
}

Like PostgreSQL’s, it settles only an invoice still pending:

func (s *store) settle(id uuid.UUID, set func(*invoice)) (bool, error) {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	if s.settleErr != nil {
		return false, s.settleErr
	}
	for _, inv := range s.invoices {
		if inv.ID == id && inv.state == "pending" {
			set(inv)
			return true, nil
		}
	}
	return false, nil
}

item.description:
The image

The image builds a static binary and runs it on distroless, as a user that isn’t root. It is built from the repository’s root, because the module replaces humus with ../..:

FROM docker.io/library/golang:1.27.2-trixie@sha256:47667934874913a449b96faa7ef4777fa285d9ec29126ee80ed61c45b7cccf0e AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY go.mod go.sum ./
COPY example/billing/go.mod example/billing/go.sum example/billing/
RUN go -C example/billing mod download
COPY . .
RUN CGO_ENABLED=0 go -C example/billing build -trimpath -ldflags=-s -o /out/billing .

FROM gcr.io/distroless/static-debian13:nonroot@sha256:e2e927ec666bae08560abb3c55d0659eceabb657f56b6782ab500a9fc7f555e3
COPY --from=build /out/billing /billing
USER 65532:65532
ENTRYPOINT ["/billing"]

docker build --file example/billing/Dockerfile --tag billing .

The CronJob

item.title: Testing
item.description:
A unit test of the Processor

The worker takes the provider and its Publishers as interfaces:

type Provider interface {
	Send(ctx context.Context, r mail.Request) (provider.Result, error)
}

type Publisher interface {
	Publish(ctx context.Context, m rabbitmq.Publishing) error
}

So its unit tests give it fakes. A fake Publisher records what it was given, and fails when the test says so:

type fakePublisher struct {
	mu sync.Mutex
	fail func(rabbitmq.Publishing) error
	published []rabbitmq.Publishing
}

func (p *fakePublisher) Publish(_ context.Context, m rabbitmq.Publishing) error {
	p.mu.Lock()
	defer p.mu.Unlock()
	p.published = append(p.published, m)
	if p.fail != nil {
		return p.fail(m)
	}
	return nil
}

func failing(exchange string, err error) func(rabbitmq.Publishing) error {
	return func(m rabbitmq.Publishing) error {
		if m.Exchange == exchange {
			return err
		}
		return nil
	}
}

A harness builds the worker on the fakes, with humustest’s telemetry:

item.title: Testing
item.description:
A unit test of the projector

The projector takes the store and its Producers as interfaces, so its unit tests give it fakes. A store in memory holds what it was given, and fails when the test says so:

type memoryStore struct {
	mu sync.Mutex
	events []store.Event
	applied []applied

	appliedErrs []error
	eventsErrs []error
	applyErrs []error

	appliedErr error
	eventsErr error

	appliedCalls int
	eventsCalls int
	applyCalls int
}

func (s *memoryStore) Apply(ctx context.Context, e store.Event, status store.Status) error {
	s.mu.Lock()
	defer s.mu.Unlock()
	s.applyCalls++
	if err := next(&s.applyErrs); err != nil {
		return err
	}
	s.events = append(s.events, e)
	s.applied = append(s.applied, applied{event: e, status: status})
	return nil
}

item.title: Observing
item.description:
Grafana

On kind, Grafana’s admin password is in the Secret up.sh made. Forward its port, and sign in as admin at http://localhost:3000:

kubectl --namespace billing get secret grafana --output jsonpath='{.data.password}' | base64 --decode
kubectl --namespace billing port-forward service/grafana 3000

A run’s trace

Each run is a trace. Its root is the job span, or a child of the trace in TRACEPARENT when whatever started the run set one. Under it are an issue span, a charge span for each invoice, and a POST span for each attempt at the payments API. In Explore, Tempo finds the runs with:

{resource.service.name="mailer" && span.messaging.message.id="<MessageId>"}
Span What it is
process mail.send the delivery, a child of the span that published the request
POST each attempt at the provider, under process mail.send
send mail.events the mail.sent or mail.refused event

item.title: Production-ready
item.description:
Every setting is sourced and checked

config.Struct sources every setting, and each one’s check names its variable. A bad one exits 78:

Period: r.Get(env("BILLING_PERIOD").Parse(parseMonth).Default(lastMonth(time.Now())).Validate(checkEnded)),
Concurrency: r.Get(env("BILLING_CONCURRENCY").Parse(strconv.Atoi).Default(4).Validate(checkConcurrency)),

The pod failure policy fails the Job on 78, with no retry:

- action: FailJob
 onExitCodes:
 containerName: billing
 operator: In
 values: [78]

No secret is in the environment, the logs or the spans

The database URL and the API key are files from Secrets, read through the Host:

item.title: Production-ready
item.description:
The mailer meets each item. Check your own worker against them:

Item How Where
Every setting sourced and checked; a bad one exits 78, naming its variable config.Struct and the packages’ checks The settings
No secret in the environment, the logs or the spans the RabbitMQ password, the provider’s key and the probes’ certificate are files read through s.Host.FS The secrets, as files
Certificates renewed without a restart the probes’ certificate is served through GetCertificate, by a small helper of the walkthrough’s own that reads its files again when they change The probes
No personal data in the telemetry addresses and bodies are never logged or put on a span What it records
Two replicas, competing for one queue a PodDisruptionBudget of minAvailable: 1 The disruption budget
Ready only once it consumes Consuming as readiness, on a probes server The probes
A rollout loses nothing, and sends nothing twice SIGTERM cancels the consumer, finishes the deliveries in flight within 25s, and nacks the rest, which counts nothing against them. terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 35 The grace period
A broker’s rolling restart costs no restart the Service reconnects. The deliveries that were in flight are redelivered, and the idempotency key sends them once The request and its key
A dependency’s outage is ridden out the client’s retries, then the delay queue, then the parking lot after MAIL_MAX_ATTEMPTS. The breaker sheds calls while the provider keeps failing Retries and dead letters
No request stops the worker malformed requests go to the parking lot at once. The rest are parked in mail.send.retry, an event that can’t be published included, and dead-lettered after MAIL_MAX_ATTEMPTS. Only a request that can go to neither mail.retry nor mail.dead stops the worker, and the delivery limit dead-letters it after 5 deliveries The delivery limit
Least privilege no configure permission on the broker; write and read on its own exchanges and queue only, granted with rabbitmqctl set_permissions. No service account token. A non-root, read-only container The logins, The Deployment
Observable traces, logs and metrics over OTLP, and the alerts in deploy/alerts.yaml Observing
Failures say why each dead letter’s reason headers, and the mail.refused event Dead letters, The events
Failures are rehearsed the failure injection cases The failure injection cases
Safe by default TrustScenario trusts no publisher; the sender’s address is a setting TrustScenario

item.title: Production-ready
item.description:
The processor meets each item. Check your own processor against them:

Item How Where
Every setting sourced and checked; a bad one exits 78, naming its variable config.Struct and the packages’ checks The settings
No secret in the environment, the logs or the spans the client certificate, PostgreSQL’s password and the probes’ key are files read through s.Host.FS. The record’s key, an order’s ID, isn’t recorded, as queue/kafka doesn’t record it The secrets, as files, A record’s trace
Certificates renewed without a restart the Kafka client certificate is served through GetClientCertificate, and the probes’ through GetCertificate, by a small helper of the walkthrough’s own that reads their files again when they change mTLS to Kafka
Concurrency within the partitions three replicas on twelve partitions; a PodDisruptionBudget of maxUnavailable: 1 Partitions, The disruption budget
Ready only once it has joined its group Joined as readiness, on an HTTPS probes port The probes
A rollout loses nothing the revoke commits the record in flight. A record’s work fits in 15s, under the 20s grace period, and terminationGracePeriodSeconds is 30. A retried record still waiting at SIGTERM is cut short when the grace period runs out, and processed again by its partition’s next owner. The rollout case checks it The deadline, main, The cases, in process
Redelivery is harmless every event applied is kept, by its partition and offset, and skipped when it comes again Skipping what was applied
No record stops it records that are malformed or of an unknown type are dead letters at once. The rest go through orders.retry, and then to orders.dlq Processing a record
An outage blocks neither topic, and keeps order its records wait in orders.retry. An order’s later events follow its earlier ones there, since an event out of order is retried too Retrying a record
Least privilege mTLS with ACLs that let it read orders.events and orders.retry, and write orders.status, orders.retry and orders.dlq. A role with three privileges on two tables. No service account token. A non-root, read-only container The ACLs, The schema, The Deployment
Observable traces from producer to orders.status, logs and metrics over OTLP, and rules for lag, a stalled group, a crash loop, dead letters, retries, an open breaker and slow processing Observing
Failures are rehearsed the failure injection cases The failure injection cases
Safe by default no record’s scenario trusted. Only the producer to orders.retry forwards one Trusting a topic’s scenarios, The Producers
